stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood into the aorta?

options.content: Right atrium
options.rationale: The right atrium receives blood from the vena cava.

options.content: Right ventricle
options.rationale: The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary artery.

options.content: Left atrium
options.rationale: The left atrium receives blood from the pulmonary veins and passes it to the left ventricle.

options.content: Left ventricle
options.rationale: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta, to the body.

explanation: The left ventricle, the chamber with the thickest wall, pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta, which carries it to the whole body.
hints: The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body.

stem: What is the function of the valves in the heart?

options.content: To stop blood flowing backwards
options.rationale: Valves keep blood flowing in one direction.

options.content: To pump blood out of the heart
options.rationale: The muscular walls pump the blood; valves only open and close.

options.content: To add oxygen to the blood
options.rationale: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs.

options.content: To supply the heart muscle with glucose
options.rationale: The coronary arteries do this.

explanation: Valves open to let blood through in the right direction and close when blood tries to flow back, so blood keeps flowing one way through the heart.
hints: Valves are like one-way doors.

stem: True or false: the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. It carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the blood picks up oxygen there.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, but not always oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen; the pulmonary veins bring it back.
hints: Blood goes to the lungs to collect oxygen.

stem: Which blood vessel brings deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium?

options.content: Aorta
options.rationale: The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the left ventricle.

options.content: Vena cava
options.rationale: The vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the body.

options.content: Pulmonary vein
options.rationale: The pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

options.content: Pulmonary artery
options.rationale: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

explanation: Deoxygenated blood from the body returns to the right atrium in the vena cava (there are two: one from the upper body and one from the lower body).
hints: It is the largest vein in the body.

stem: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle?

options.content: It pumps a larger volume of blood with each beat.
options.rationale: Both ventricles pump the same volume of blood.

options.content: It has to pump blood to the lungs, which are a long way away.
options.rationale: The right ventricle pumps blood to the nearby lungs.

options.content: It pumps blood at a higher pressure, all round the body.
options.rationale: Higher pressure needs a stronger, thicker muscle.

options.content: It receives deoxygenated blood, which is harder to pump.
options.rationale: The left ventricle receives oxygenated blood; oxygen does not change how hard blood is to pump.

explanation: The left ventricle must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, so it needs a thick, strong muscular wall. The right ventricle pumps the same volume only to the lungs, at a lower pressure.
hints: Think about where each ventricle sends its blood.

stem: Name the blood vessels that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen and glucose.

rejected.feedback: The coronary arteries branch from the aorta, but the aorta itself does not supply the heart muscle.
The vena cava returns blood from the body.
The pulmonary artery takes blood to the lungs.

explanation: The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and spread over the surface of the heart, supplying the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose for respiration.
hints: Their name comes from a word meaning 'crown', because they circle the heart.

stem: Complete the path of blood through the heart and lungs.

payload.template: vena cava → right atrium → {{blank:rv}} → {{blank:pa}} → lungs → {{blank:pv}} → left atrium → left ventricle → {{blank:ao}} → body

explanation: Blood flows vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
hints: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring it back.

stem: What is meant by a **double circulation**?

options.content: The body has two hearts, one pumping blood to each of the two lungs.
options.rationale: There is one heart with two sides.

options.content: Blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body.
options.rationale: Once through the pulmonary circulation and once through the systemic circulation.

options.content: Blood flows round the body twice as fast as it does in the body of a fish.
options.rationale: The word 'double' refers to passing through the heart twice.

options.content: Each blood vessel has two layers of muscle.
options.rationale: This has nothing to do with the circulation.

explanation: In a double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: right side → lungs → left side (pulmonary circulation), then left side → body → right side (systemic circulation).
hints: Count how many times blood passes through the heart in one trip round the body.

stem: What is the main advantage of the double circulation of a mammal?

options.content: Blood does not need to go to the lungs.
options.rationale: Blood must still pass through the lungs to collect oxygen.

options.content: The heart needs fewer chambers.
options.rationale: A mammal's heart has four chambers, more than a fish's.

options.content: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are mixed in the heart to give an even supply of oxygen.
options.rationale: The septum keeps them separate.

options.content: Blood returning from the lungs is pumped again, so it reaches the body at high pressure.
options.rationale: This delivers oxygen and glucose to the tissues quickly.

explanation: In a double circulation, blood that has lost pressure passing through the lung capillaries returns to the heart and is pumped again. It reaches the body at high pressure and flows quickly, delivering oxygen and glucose fast enough for an active mammal, while the lungs receive blood at a gentler, lower pressure.
hints: What happens to blood pressure after blood passes through capillaries?

stem: Which describes the route of blood in the single circulation of a fish?

options.content: Heart → gills → body → heart
options.rationale: Blood passes through the heart once per circuit.

options.content: Heart → body → heart → gills → heart
options.rationale: This would be a double circulation.

options.content: Gills → heart → body → gills
options.rationale: Blood goes from the heart to the gills, not from the gills to the heart.

options.content: Heart → lungs → heart → body → heart
options.rationale: Fish have gills, and this route is a double circulation.

explanation: A fish's heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills, where it picks up oxygen. The blood then flows on round the body and back to the heart, passing through the heart only once per circuit.
hints: In a single circulation, the blood passes through the heart once per circuit.

stem: Sipho counts 23 pulse beats in 20 seconds. Calculate his heart rate in beats per minute.
explanation: There are three 20-second periods in a minute, so heart rate $= 23 \times 3 = 69$ beats per minute.
workedSolution:
1. $60 \div 20 = 3$ periods of 20 s in one minute.
2. $23 \times 3 = 69$ beats per minute.
hints: How many 20-second periods are there in one minute?

stem: Rudo's resting heart rate is 64 beats per minute. Immediately after a 400 m race it is 144 beats per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in her heart rate.
explanation: Increase $= 144 - 64 = 80$ beats per minute. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{80}{64} \times 100 = 125\%$.
hints: Divide the increase by the resting value, not by the final value.

stem: What happens to the valves when the ventricles contract?

options.content: The atrioventricular valves open and the semilunar valves close.
options.rationale: This is the wrong way round: it would push blood back into the atria.

options.content: Both sets of valves open.
options.rationale: If the atrioventricular valves were open, blood would flow back into the atria.

options.content: The atrioventricular valves close and the semilunar valves open.
options.rationale: Blood is forced into the arteries and cannot flow back into the atria.

options.content: Both sets of valves close.
options.rationale: Blood must be able to leave the ventricles.

explanation: As the ventricles contract, the pressure inside them rises. This closes the atrioventricular valves (preventing backflow into the atria) and opens the semilunar valves, so blood is forced into the aorta and pulmonary artery.
hints: Where must the blood go when the ventricles squeeze, and where must it not go?

stem: A doctor listens to the heart with a stethoscope and hears a 'lub-dub' sound with each beat. What causes the 'lub' sound?

options.content: The ventricles filling with blood
options.rationale: Filling is quiet; the sounds come from valves closing.

options.content: The atrioventricular valves closing as the ventricles start to contract
options.rationale: The first sound is these valves snapping shut.

options.content: Blood rushing through the coronary arteries as the heart muscle contracts
options.rationale: The heart sounds are made by valves closing.

options.content: The semilunar valves opening as the ventricles start to empty
options.rationale: The second sound ('dub') is made when the semilunar valves close.

explanation: The 'lub' is the atrioventricular valves closing as the ventricles begin to contract; the 'dub' is the semilunar valves closing as the ventricles relax.
hints: The heart sounds are made by valves closing.

stem: Which method records the electrical activity of the heart?

options.content: Counting the pulse at the wrist
options.rationale: This measures heart rate, not electrical activity.

options.content: Listening with a stethoscope
options.rationale: This detects the sounds of the valves closing.

options.content: Measuring blood pressure with a cuff
options.rationale: This measures pressure in the arteries.

options.content: An electrocardiogram (ECG)
options.rationale: Electrodes on the skin record the heart's electrical activity as a trace.

explanation: An electrocardiogram (ECG) uses electrodes on the skin to record the electrical changes in the heart muscle as it beats. Pulse rate and heart sounds are other ways of monitoring the heart.
hints: Its abbreviation is three letters, beginning with E.

stem: Why is the septum of the heart important?

options.content: It keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart, so they do not mix.
options.rationale: Without it, the two would mix.

options.content: It pumps blood into the aorta.
options.rationale: The ventricles pump blood; the septum separates them.

options.content: It stops blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles.
options.rationale: The semilunar valves do this.

options.content: It carries oxygen to the heart muscle.
options.rationale: The coronary arteries do this.

explanation: The septum separates the right side of the heart (deoxygenated blood) from the left side (oxygenated blood). Keeping them apart means the blood pumped to the body is fully oxygenated.
hints: The septum is the wall between the left and right sides.

stem: Match each part of the heart with its function.

right.content: Receives deoxygenated blood from the body
Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs
Pumps blood to the rest of the body
Stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles
Carry oxygen and glucose to the heart muscle

explanation: The right atrium receives blood from the body and the left atrium from the lungs; the right ventricle pumps to the lungs and the left ventricle to the body; the semilunar valves stop backflow from the arteries. The coronary arteries (not listed) supply the heart muscle.
hints: Atria receive blood; ventricles pump it out.

stem:
Chipo, who trains for athletics, and Nyasha, who does not, each did three minutes of step-ups. Their pulse rates (beats per minute) were measured at rest and at one-minute intervals after the exercise.

|  | At rest | 0 min after | 1 min | 2 min | 3 min | 4 min | 5 min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chipo | 64 | 118 | 96 | 78 | 66 | 64 | 64 |
| Nyasha | 78 | 152 | 138 | 120 | 104 | 92 | 84 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the increase in Nyasha's pulse rate between rest and the end of the exercise.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How many minutes after the exercise did Chipo's pulse rate return to her resting rate?

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the pulse rate increases during exercise.

points.description: Muscles contract more, so they respire (aerobically) faster
They need more oxygen and glucose
and produce more carbon dioxide that must be removed
The heart beats faster to deliver oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide more quickly

parts.explanation: During exercise the muscles contract more and respire faster. They need more oxygen and glucose, and they make more carbon dioxide. The heart beats faster, so blood delivers oxygen and glucose to the muscles and carries carbon dioxide away more quickly.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** reasons for the differences between Chipo's and Nyasha's results.

points.description: Chipo is fitter / trains regularly
Her heart muscle is stronger and pumps more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats
So her resting rate is lower, her rate rises less and she recovers faster

parts.explanation: Chipo trains, so her heart muscle is stronger and pumps more blood with each beat. Her heart needs fewer beats to supply the same oxygen, so her resting rate is lower, it rises less during exercise and it returns to normal faster.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** variables that should be kept the same to make the comparison fair.

points.description: Type, duration (3 minutes) or rate / height of the step-ups
Resting for the same time before starting / measuring the pulse the same way and for the same time / similar age, sex or body mass

parts.explanation: For example: the same step height, rate and duration of exercise, and the same way of measuring the pulse (same length of count) after the same rest beforehand.

explanation: (a) $152 - 78 = 74$ beats per minute. (b) Chipo's rate was back to 64 four minutes after the exercise. Exercise raises the rate because respiring muscles need more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide. A trained athlete's stronger heart pumps more blood per beat, so her rate is lower, rises less and recovers sooner.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $152 - 78 = 74$ beats per minute.
2. (b) Chipo: 64 at rest, and 64 again at 4 min, so 4 minutes.
hints: Recovery time is when the rate first returns to the resting value.
Link the heart rate to respiration in the muscles.

stem:
A student describes the labelled parts of a diagram of the heart, viewed from the front.

| Label | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | Chamber at the top right of the diagram that receives blood from four veins coming from the lungs |
| B | Chamber at the bottom right of the diagram with the thickest muscular wall |
| C | Large vessel leaving the top of B and arching over the heart |
| D | Chamber at the bottom left of the diagram, with a thinner wall than B |
| E | Wall of muscle between B and D |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each label with the name of the structure.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The left side of the heart appears on the right of the diagram. Why?

options.content: Because the diagram shows the heart as if the person were facing you
options.rationale: Their left is on your right.

options.content: Because the heart is on the right side of the body
options.rationale: The heart lies slightly to the left in the chest.

options.content: Because the left side of the heart has a thicker, larger muscular wall
options.rationale: Size has nothing to do with which side of the page it is drawn on.

options.content: Because blood from the body enters the heart on the right side
options.rationale: This is not why diagrams are drawn this way.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the wall of B is thicker than the wall of D.

points.description: B (left ventricle) pumps blood all round the body / D (right ventricle) only to the lungs
so B must produce a higher pressure (needs more muscle)

parts.explanation: B is the left ventricle, which pumps blood around the whole body, so it must produce a much higher pressure than D, the right ventricle, which pumps blood only to the nearby lungs.

explanation: A is the left atrium (it receives the pulmonary veins), B the left ventricle (thickest wall), C the aorta, D the right ventricle and E the septum. Diagrams show the heart as if the person is facing you. The left ventricle pumps blood at a higher pressure round the whole body.
hints: Which chamber has the thickest wall?
The pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs.

stem: Describe how the heart pumps blood during one heartbeat. Include the actions of the atria, the ventricles and the valves. [6]

points.description: Atria fill with blood from the veins (vena cava and pulmonary veins)
Atria contract, pushing blood through the (open) atrioventricular valves into the ventricles
Ventricles contract, raising the pressure inside them
Atrioventricular valves close, preventing backflow into the atria
Semilunar valves open; blood is pushed into the aorta and pulmonary artery
Ventricles relax; semilunar valves close, preventing backflow from the arteries
Both sides contract together; the left ventricle produces the higher pressure

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The atria relax and fill with blood: deoxygenated blood from the vena cava enters the right atrium and oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins enters the left atrium. The atria then contract, pushing blood through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. Next the ventricles contract. The pressure inside them rises, so the atrioventricular valves close, preventing blood flowing back into the atria, and the semilunar valves open, so blood is forced into the pulmonary artery and the aorta. The ventricles then relax; as their pressure falls, the semilunar valves close and stop blood flowing back from the arteries. The two sides contract at the same time, but the thicker left ventricle produces a higher pressure.

explanation: A full answer gives the sequence (atria fill, atria contract, ventricles contract, ventricles relax) and says which valves open or close at each stage and why.
hints: Start with the atria filling and end with the ventricles relaxing.
At each stage, say which valves are open or closed.

stem: A woman's heart beats at an average of 75 beats per minute. How many times does it beat in one day?
explanation: Beats per hour $= 75 \times 60 = 4500$; beats per day $= 4500 \times 24 = 108\,000$.
workedSolution:
1. Beats per hour: $75 \times 60 = 4500$.
2. Beats per day: $4500 \times 24 = 108\,000$.
hints: There are 60 minutes in an hour and 24 hours in a day.

stem: True or false: the right ventricle pumps blood at a lower pressure than the left ventricle.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. The right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs, at a lower pressure that does not damage the lung capillaries.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. The right ventricle has a thinner wall and pumps blood only to the nearby lungs, at a lower pressure.

explanation: The right ventricle pumps blood a short distance to the lungs at low pressure, so its wall is thinner than the left ventricle's, which pumps at high pressure to the whole body. Both pump the same volume.
hints: Compare the thickness of the two ventricle walls.

stem:
The table shows the blood pressure in the left atrium, the left ventricle and the aorta at five moments during one heartbeat.

| Time / s | 0.0 | 0.1 | 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Left atrium / kPa | 1.0 | 1.3 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 1.0 |
| Left ventricle / kPa | 0.8 | 1.2 | 16.0 | 6.0 | 0.6 |
| Aorta / kPa | 10.5 | 10.0 | 15.5 | 12.5 | 11.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which valves are open at 0.2 s?

options.content: The atrioventricular valve only
options.rationale: The ventricle pressure (16.0 kPa) is far above the atrium pressure, so this valve is shut.

options.content: Both valves
options.rationale: The atrioventricular valve is pushed shut by the high ventricle pressure.

options.content: The semilunar valve only
options.rationale: Ventricle pressure (16.0) is above aorta pressure (15.5), so blood is pushed into the aorta.

options.content: Neither valve
options.rationale: Blood is being pumped into the aorta, so the semilunar valve must be open.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: At 0.3 s, which valves are closed?

options.content: The atrioventricular valve only
options.rationale: The ventricle pressure (6.0) is also below the aorta pressure (12.5).

options.content: The semilunar valve only
options.rationale: The ventricle pressure (6.0) is still above the atrium pressure (0.8).

options.content: Both the atrioventricular and semilunar valves
options.rationale: The ventricle is relaxing: its pressure is below the aorta's but above the atrium's.

options.content: Neither the atrioventricular nor the semilunar valve
options.rationale: Blood is not flowing in or out of the ventricle at this moment.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: At 0.2 s, by how much is the pressure in the left ventricle greater than the pressure in the left atrium?

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the atrioventricular valve closes when the ventricle contracts, and why this is important.

points.description: The pressure in the ventricle rises above the pressure in the atrium, pushing the valve shut
This stops blood flowing back into the atrium, so it is forced into the aorta

parts.explanation: When the ventricle contracts, its pressure rises above that in the atrium, which pushes the atrioventricular valve shut. This prevents backflow into the atrium, so blood can only leave through the aorta.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest how the highest pressure in the right ventricle would compare with the highest pressure in the left ventricle, and why.

points.description: Lower, because the right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs (thinner wall / lungs are close and delicate)

parts.explanation: It would be lower, because the right ventricle has a thinner wall and pumps blood only to the nearby lungs, whose capillaries would be damaged by high pressure.

explanation: Valves open when the pressure behind them is higher than in front. At 0.2 s the ventricle (16.0 kPa) is above the aorta (15.5 kPa), so the semilunar valve is open, and far above the atrium (0.6 kPa), so the atrioventricular valve is shut: $16.0 - 0.6 = 15.4$ kPa. At 0.3 s the ventricle (6.0) is below the aorta (12.5) but above the atrium (0.8), so both valves are closed.
hints: A valve is pushed open when the pressure behind it is greater than the pressure in front of it.
Compare the ventricle with the atrium for one valve, and with the aorta for the other.
